extracted.intended_audience: writers and editors (journalists) and anyone who writes
extracted.subtask_description: A usage and style manual (New York Times Manual of Style and Usage, 5th ed.) intended as an authoritative, quick-reference guide for journalists and other writers on spelling, grammar, punctuation, word choice, and internet-era usage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Hyphenation, punctuation, capitalization and spelling
rubrics_metrics.description: The guidelines to hyphenation, punctuation, capitalization and spelling are crisp and compact, created for instant reference in the rush of daily deadlines.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides definitive guidance on when and how to hyphenate, punctuate, capitalize, and spell words; written to be concise for quick look-up during deadline-driven work. Example topical contrasts on the page: 'Lay or lie? Who or whom? That or which?'

rubrics_metrics.name: Answers to knotty usage and meaning questions
rubrics_metrics.description: For anyone who writes—short stories or business plans, book reports or news articles—knotty choices of spelling, grammar, punctuation and meaning lurk in every line.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Addresses tricky usage questions and distinctions of meaning and form (examples given: 'Does the White House tweet? Or does the White House post on Twitter?', 'Can “text” be a verb and also a noun?', 'When should you link?'). Intended to resolve everyday writing dilemmas.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alphabetical, handy reference format
rubrics_metrics.description: A handy alphabetical guide used by the writers and editors of the world’s most authoritative news organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organized alphabetically for quick look-up; designed as a practical desk reference rather than exhaustive scholarly treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Internet-age usage and citation guidance
rubrics_metrics.description: Updated with solutions to problems that plague writers in the Internet age.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes specific guidance on digital-era issues such as how to cite links and blogs, and when/how to include hyperlinks or references to online sources in journalistic writing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Handling social-media content (tweets, hashtags, etc.)
rubrics_metrics.description: How to handle tweets, hashtags and other social-media content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Offers rules and examples for quoting, attributing, formatting, and integrating social-media content into reporting and writing, reflecting current newsroom practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Guidance on contemporary and inclusive terminology
rubrics_metrics.description: How to use current terms like 'transgender,' or to choose thoughtfully between 'same-sex marriage' and 'gay marriage'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provides recommendations for current, sensitive, and inclusive word choice; emphasizes thoughtful selection of terms depending on context and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Conciseness and usability under deadline pressure
rubrics_metrics.description: Guidelines are described as 'crisp and compact' and intended 'for instant reference in the rush of daily deadlines.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prioritizes brevity and clarity so guidance can be applied quickly in newsroom conditions; the book's format and tone favor actionable rules and short examples rather than lengthy exposition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Authoritative editorial provenance
rubrics_metrics.description: The Official Style Guide Used by the Writers and Editors of the World's Most Authoritative News Organization.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because of its provenance (NYT editors), the guide functions as an authoritative newsroom standard; users can rely on it as the basis for editorial decisions and consistency across reporting.
